{"self_assessment": "Impact: I laid the lower tail piece early, and it connected to the run and was live to the tip. I then built the bottom body line from the tail crossing forward toward Maya's line and laid the join across to her end, which tied the lower body into the run. Late on, I fixed the jammed dominoes on the upper tail and lifted the stray pale dominoes past the tail so the supply went back to the pile when the table had run out. That let Maya keep closing the notch. At the push, the start run reached roughly 199 of the 248 standing dominoes, so most of the fish was connected.

Execution: I worked in the order the run needed. I did the tail first, then the body from the crossing, then the joins as the neighbouring lines arrived. Near the end I switched to inspection and small fixes rather than adding new pieces. I read the table to tell which pale pieces were harmless strays and which were real open ends, such as the unclosed notch at the upper tail tip. That kept effort on what the judge would see.

Collaboration: I told people when I was coming toward their line, asked where they had stopped before making joins, and offered help on the body. I kept my hands off the notch while Maya was working there so we would not bump each other. I gave Tom a view of the tail tip from my side, and I released dominoes back to the shared pile when the table ran dry.

Leadership: I kept the status of the joins and open ends visible to the table. I flagged the two-minute mark and asked for a go-ahead before touching a spot someone else was working. I also made clear who owned each piece, to avoid duplicated work and collisions in the last minutes. Priya set the overall plan and I supported it.

I think the table's result was a team effort, with my contribution around a fifth of it.", "my_share_percent": 20}
